whyCorrect: The passage says most of the sound is thrown away, and that what survives is just enough for a listener who already knows the topic. So the listener is supplying the missing pieces from context — building the full message back out of a stripped-down signal. "Reconstruct" is exactly that operation, and it is the only choice that accounts for the fact that information was lost.

whyWrong.B: The whistle is Spanish, not a second language, so there is nothing to translate between; the listener recovers Spanish from Spanish.
whyWrong.C: Amplify concerns loudness, and the sentence is about missing information, not a weak signal. The text already says the whistle carries across a ravine.
whyWrong.D: Record means to preserve what is there, which does nothing about the parts of the sound that were discarded.

tips: When a blank follows a sentence about information being lost, look for a word meaning to restore or infer what is gone.

whyCorrect: The sentence turns on a contrast: cable was laid for telecommunications, and it has turned out to be something else — good for detecting lorries and earthquakes. The blank therefore needs a positive word meaning "usable for this job." "Serviceable as a seismic array" says the idle fibre does useful work in a role it was never intended for.

whyWrong.A: Expendable means fit to be used up or discarded, which is the opposite of the point that the unused fibre has found a valuable second use.
whyWrong.B: Unnecessary describes the fibre's original telecom role, but the blank sits in the clause about the new seismic role, where the fibre is clearly needed.
whyWrong.C: Conspicuous means easily noticed; buried fibre under a street is not being described as visible, and visibility would not make it a seismic array.

commonMistakes: Choices A and B both echo "more fibre than the traffic required" and feel on-topic, but the blank describes the new use, not the surplus.

whyCorrect: Every detail before the blank is about air: the tower is hollow, sun and shade drive air up one set of channels and down another, and the flow carries off carbon dioxide. That is gas exchange, and the colony itself lives elsewhere. "Lung" is the metaphor that matches breathing, and it completes the contrast with "dwelling" because a lung is an organ, not a residence.

whyWrong.A: Fortress implies defence against attackers, which the passage never mentions; the tower is described as hollow and empty rather than protective.
whyWrong.C: Granary implies stored food, but the text places the fungus gardens in the underground nest and says the tower is largely empty.
whyWrong.D: Monument implies something built to commemorate or display, whereas every detail given is functional.

tips: When the sentence has the shape "less an X than a _____," the blank must contrast with X — here, something that works rather than something lived in.

whyCorrect: The described design removes the one thing readers misjudge: nothing is ever drawn larger, so the eye counts identical figures instead of comparing areas. The point of that rule is that a reader cannot misread the quantity. "Unambiguous" names that property, and it fits the closing phrase about a reader with no training at all.

whyWrong.A: Compact means small or space-saving, but repeating one figure many times makes a chart longer, not smaller.
whyWrong.B: Provisional means temporary or subject to revision, which has nothing to do with how the chart is read.
whyWrong.D: Decorative would work against the passage, which presents the repeated figure as a device for accuracy rather than for appearance.

commonMistakes: Students pick "compact" because the figures are described as small; the sentence is about clarity for an untrained reader, not size.

whyCorrect: The sentences before define the word for you: the channel was dredged to five metres, a container hull "needs seven metres beneath it," and a ship that touches bottom is worthless. So the underlined word names the depth of water a vessel requires in order to stay afloat, which is why it, and not quay length, decided which ports survived.

whyWrong.A: This is the drinking sense of the word, unrelated to a passage about hulls and channel depth.
whyWrong.B: This is the moving-air sense of the word; it is a real meaning but nothing in the passage concerns air.
whyWrong.D: This is the "first version of a document" sense, spelled the same way in British usage, but no writing is discussed.

tips: For an underlined-word question, find the sentence that supplies a number or a definition — here "needs seven metres beneath it" fixes the meaning.

whyCorrect: The text closes by saying the linguists describe a language that was made rather than taught. The underlined sentence supplies the evidence for that: the youngest pupils produced regularities their teachers and older schoolmates did not have, so the grammar could not have been passed down to them. Its function is to give the observation the final claim rests on.

whyWrong.A: The sentence states that the older pupils were signing; it says only that they lacked the younger pupils' regularities.
whyWrong.B: The reason the children were taught at home — isolation before the schools opened — is given in the first sentence, not the underlined one.
whyWrong.C: Recording methods are mentioned in the last sentence, and even there only that both groups were recorded; the underlined sentence describes what the children did.

commonMistakes: Function questions are answered by asking what the sentence does for the argument, not by finding which choice restates it most accurately.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence says a turf wall settles, which forces the roof timbers to be taken down and reset every few decades. The next sentence reports that houses were rebuilt on the same spot so often that the mound is metres deep. So the underlined sentence supplies the cause of the repeated rebuilding that the closing sentence describes.

whyWrong.A: The loss of woodland is stated in the first sentence as background; the underlined sentence treats scarce timber as a consequence of that loss, not an explanation of it.
whyWrong.B: No comparison of turf with stone is made — the passage says bare stone holds no heat, which is a reason turf was chosen, and the underlined sentence makes no judgement of quality.
whyWrong.C: The herringbone cutting of the blocks is described in the previous sentence; the underlined sentence is about what happens to a finished wall over time.

tips: When an underlined sentence is followed by a result, its function is usually to set up that result.

whyCorrect: The passage lists three features — combs, fringe, velvet pile — and gives one shared job for all of them: each breaks up turbulent air that would otherwise hiss. The last sentence is the control case: owls that chase insects in open air, where silence buys nothing, have none of the three. That combination makes the main idea about noise reduction, not speed or anything else.

whyWrong.A: The final sentence rules this out: fast insect-hunting owls lack all three structures, so quietness is not a property of all owls.
whyWrong.B: Warmth is never mentioned; the pile is introduced only as one of the three structures that break up turbulent air.
whyWrong.D: The text compares the owl's wingbeat to the hearing threshold of mice, which is a fact about the sound level, not about how well owls hear.

commonMistakes: Choice A turns a claim about particular owls into a claim about all of them — main-idea distractors are often the passage's point stretched past what it supports.

whyCorrect: The relevant sentence says that in a dry year the shortage is shared rather than allocated by seniority, and then states the mechanism: every turn is shortened by the same fraction. So each household loses the same proportion of its water and the shortfall lands on all of them together.

whyWrong.B: Buying water from another association is never mentioned; the mayordomo's stated role is setting the rotation.
whyWrong.C: Labour is owed in proportion to the water a household already draws, so it is an obligation that follows the allotment rather than a way of deciding who gets water in a drought.
whyWrong.D: The passage explicitly rejects this: the shortage is shared "rather than allocated by seniority."

tips: When a passage names what it is not doing, the rejected option is almost always one of the choices.

whyCorrect: Aalto's claim is causal and it has a rival: survival comes from the glucose flood, not from tough tissue. The finding that supports her has to remove the glucose and show survival fails. Frogs whose livers could not release glucose dying at temperatures untreated frogs survived does exactly that, since the tissues were unchanged and only the glucose was taken away.

whyWrong.A: A wide northern range shows wood frogs tolerate cold but says nothing about which mechanism produces the tolerance, which is the whole disagreement.
whyWrong.B: Repeated freezing and thawing again shows how well the frogs endure freezing without identifying glucose as the reason.
whyWrong.D: The temperature at which freezing begins is about when ice forms, not about what protects the frog once it has formed.

tips: For a support-the-hypothesis question, ask which finding would come out differently if the hypothesis were false.

whyCorrect: Ferrand's claim sets the cave environment against a cave-specific mould, so the useful finding separates the two. Choice B does: with a laboratory mould held constant, the caves still produce traditional cheese and a warehouse does not, which pins the character on airflow and humidity rather than on any special local strain.

whyWrong.A: Long historical use of the caves shows the method is old, not which of the two candidate causes is doing the work.
whyWrong.C: A distinct species name for the cave mould supports the rival explanation Ferrand is arguing against.
whyWrong.D: The breed of sheep introduces a third factor and leaves the cave-versus-mould question untouched.

commonMistakes: Choices that are merely true about the caves feel supportive; only a comparison that varies one factor while holding the other fixed tests the claim.

whyCorrect: Raghavan's claim is specifically statistical: the sequences behave like a script encoding a language. The evidence has to be a statistical property measured against both a script benchmark and a non-language benchmark, which is what the sign-to-sign transition probabilities in choice D provide. Falling inside the range for known scripts and outside the range for emblem systems is the direct test of her claim.

whyWrong.A: How the seals were physically used fits the rival view that they mark ownership just as well, so it discriminates between nothing.
whyWrong.B: A sign inventory under five hundred is compatible with a script and with a symbol set alike; the count alone settles nothing.
whyWrong.C: A seventeen-sign sequence is a length record, not a measurement of how the signs are ordered.

tips: Match the evidence to the exact form of the claim — a statistical claim needs a statistic, not a fact about the objects.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes the physical requirement: the towers must stand within sight of one another, because the message is the visible position of the arms. Fog removes the sightline, and with it the only channel the system has. The "however" signals a reversal of the fast, efficient picture just given, so the line simply stops working.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the code book was kept only at the two ends and no keeper knew what he passed, so memorised codes contradict the text.
whyWrong.B: Nothing connects visibility to the direction of travel, and reversing direction would not help a keeper who cannot see the next tower.
whyWrong.C: This assumes the line still runs, only slower; if the arms cannot be seen at all, there is no slower rate at which the message gets through.

commonMistakes: A partial-failure answer looks safely moderate, but here the mechanism is all-or-nothing: no sightline means no signal.

whyCorrect: The passage tells you exactly what the balance requirement cannot catch — an invented sale, because a fiction entered twice still balances. So what it does catch is the case where the two sides stop matching, and that happens when a transaction is entered once instead of twice. The missing half throws the column totals out and the error shows up.

whyWrong.B: A wrong currency entered as both a debit and a credit still balances, so the totals give no signal.
whyWrong.C: Theft happens outside the book; nothing about the ledger's arithmetic reveals goods leaving a warehouse.
whyWrong.D: This is the possibility the previous sentence rules out — an invented sale is a deliberate misstatement and balances perfectly.

tips: When a text says what a system fails to detect, the blank usually names the complementary case the system does detect.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "Because," so everything through "a clear amber liquid" is a subordinate clause and the sentence still needs a main clause. "Garum tasted less of fish than of salt" is that main clause, and a subordinate clause introducing a main clause is separated from it by a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and the "Because" clause on the left is dependent.
whyWrong.B: A colon also requires an independent clause in front of it, which the "Because" clause is not.
whyWrong.C: "And" pulls "garum tasted" inside the "Because" clause, leaving the whole sentence a fragment with no main clause at all.

commonMistakes: It is easy to hear a full sentence in "the fermentation broke the fish down" and forget that "Because" makes the entire clause dependent.

whyCorrect: "Although" subordinates everything up to "in warm weather," so that stretch cannot stand alone. The independent clause is "the same stems left for a fortnight come apart in the hand," and the boundary between an opening subordinate clause and the main clause takes a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides; "Although a week in a slow river will loosen that gum in warm weather" is dependent.
whyWrong.B: A colon has the same requirement on its left side, which the "Although" clause does not meet.
whyWrong.C: "And" makes the second half part of the "Although" clause too, so the sentence becomes a fragment with no main clause.

tips: Cover the opening word: if removing "Although" would leave a sentence, the clause is dependent only because of that word, and it still needs a comma, not a semicolon.

whyCorrect: "Cutting one down the middle exposes a record of local rainfall reaching back a hundred thousand years" is a complete sentence, and so is "the layers can be dated from the uranium they contain to within a few decades." Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them are joined with a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation at all the two independent clauses run together as a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: A colon cannot be followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause explains nothing that the colon would be introducing.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Students often reach for the comma because the two statements are closely related; closeness of meaning does not license a comma between complete sentences.

whyCorrect: "Counting the pairs down a core gives a year-by-year chronology" is a complete sentence — the gerund phrase is its subject — and "a bed of volcanic ash lying at one depth ties that count to a date established somewhere else entirely" is a second complete sentence. A semicolon is the punctuation that joins two independent clauses without a conjunction.

whyWrong.A: Running the two independent clauses together with no punctuation produces a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by "and" is never correct, and the second clause adds a separate fact rather than explaining the first.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

tips: Test each half on its own: if both stand as sentences, only a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a conjunction will join them.

whyCorrect: "All four" tells you there is more than one herdsman, and the lofts belong to them, so you need the plural possessive. "Herdsmen" is already plural without an s, and an irregular plural of that kind takes an apostrophe plus s: herdsmen's.

whyWrong.A: "Herdsman's" is singular possessive, which contradicts "all four."
whyWrong.C: "Herdsmens'" adds a plural s to a word that is already plural; the apostrophe-after-s rule applies only to plurals that end in s, such as farmers'.
whyWrong.D: "Herdsmen" is a plain plural with no possessive marking, so it cannot show that the lofts belong to them.

tips: For irregular plurals — children, women, herdsmen — the possessive is always apostrophe plus s.

whyCorrect: With a "neither … nor" subject, the verb agrees with whichever noun sits closer to it, and here that is the plural "the members." The plural form is "receive." The surrounding sentences are in the present tense describing how the club runs, so the simple present is also the right tense.

whyWrong.B: "Has received" is singular and shifts to the present perfect, which breaks both the agreement with "members" and the general-present description of how the club works.
whyWrong.C: "Is receiving" is singular, and the progressive suggests something happening right now rather than a standing feature of the club.
whyWrong.D: "Receives" is the singular form, which would agree with "the organiser" rather than with the nearer noun "the members."

commonMistakes: "Neither … nor" makes students reach automatically for a singular verb; the rule is proximity, not automatic singularity.

whyCorrect: Find what "that" refers back to. The phrase is "one of the few nineteenth-century measurements that …," and the relative clause describes the whole group of measurements, not the single baseline — several measurements have been confirmed, and this baseline is one of them. A plural antecedent takes "have."

whyWrong.A: "Is been confirmed" is not a possible verb form in English.
whyWrong.B: "Has" would agree with a singular antecedent, which would require the clause to describe only the baseline rather than the group of measurements it belongs to.
whyWrong.D: "Having been confirmed" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the relative clause would have no main verb.

tips: In "one of the few X that …," the relative clause modifies X, so the verb is plural.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives two properties: the store responds within milliseconds and it leaks a few per cent an hour. The second sentence states the use those two properties dictate — seconds and minutes, not overnight. That is a result drawn from the facts just given, so the transition has to be a consequence marker.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" signals that what follows goes against the previous statement, but the short-term use follows directly from the hourly losses.
whyWrong.B: "By contrast" needs two things being compared, and only the flywheel store is under discussion.
whyWrong.C: "For example" would make the second sentence an instance of the first, but it describes an application rather than another case of fast response and leakage.

commonMistakes: The "but" inside the first sentence tempts you toward a contrast word; that contrast is already resolved before the blank.

whyCorrect: Both sentences report the same phenomenon in different settings: a person fails to notice that the human being in front of them has been swapped for someone else. The second is a parallel case, not a consequence of the first and not an opposing result, so the transition should mark the likeness.

whyWrong.B: "Consequently" claims the film finding causes the pedestrian finding, but neither experiment produces the other.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" requires the second case to come out differently, and it comes out the same way.
whyWrong.D: "In short" introduces a summary, whereas the second sentence adds a new and more specific piece of evidence.

tips: When two sentences report the same outcome in different situations, the transition marks similarity.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the two sources give an identical product. The second says one of them yields about a thirtieth as much dye, which is a disadvantage that survives despite the identical chemistry — and it is the reason woad growers wanted indigo banned. A concessive transition, marking that the second fact holds in spite of the first, is what fits.

whyWrong.A: "In particular" would make the yield a specific instance of the dyes being indistinguishable, but yield is a different property altogether.
whyWrong.C: "Therefore" claims the poor yield follows from the two dyes being identical, which reverses the relationship.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" would mean the second sentence points the same way as the first, when in fact it introduces the crucial difference between the two crops.

commonMistakes: Sameness in one respect and difference in another is the classic setup for a concessive transition, not for "similarly."

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing: the obstacle the imaging had to overcome. The obstacle in the notes is that carbon ink and carbonised papyrus have almost the same density, so the ink is invisible to a scan that measures density — and the note about texture-trained models is how it was got round. Choice B pairs the obstacle with the workaround and is the only option that mentions the difficulty at all.

whyWrong.A: The number of scrolls and the eruption are background; nothing there is an obstacle to imaging.
whyWrong.C: The destructive unrolling is the older method's failure, not a problem the imaging had to solve.
whyWrong.D: This states what the tomography does, which is the capability rather than the obstacle.

tips: A synthesis question is graded on the stated goal only — a true note that answers a different question is still wrong.

whyCorrect: The goal is the practical difficulty of building, so the sentence needs the notes that make the job hard: multi-tonne columns, a source on the opposite side of the island, and no wheel, draught animal or metal tool. Choice B is the only option that combines them, and combining them is what conveys the difficulty.

whyWrong.A: The sorcery tradition is a local explanation for how the stones moved, which sidesteps the practical difficulty rather than emphasising it.
whyWrong.C: Saying the walls are basalt columns omits their weight, the distance and the missing tools, so nothing about it is difficult.
whyWrong.D: This describes what the site is and gives no information about the effort of building it.

commonMistakes: Choices that quote a single note verbatim are usually true but too thin to meet a goal that asks you to emphasise something.

whyCorrect: The goal has two halves — reduced, and not solved — so the sentence must carry both. Choice C gives the reduction (levels have fallen since the 2019 ban) and the persistence (many birds still test above the threshold) in one sentence. No other choice contains a contrast at all.

whyWrong.A: This states the severity of the problem but says nothing about any improvement.
whyWrong.B: This explains the mechanism by which condors ingest lead and reports neither progress nor its limits.
whyWrong.D: The trapping and testing programme is a monitoring measure; it does not indicate whether lead levels have changed.

tips: When a goal contains a "but" — improved yet incomplete, cheap yet slow — the right choice contains one too.

whyCorrect: Every detail is about knowing in advance what the night will bring: the buildings stand a fixed day's march apart, each has the same layout, and the keeper answers to the ruler. The sentence also rules out the alternative explanation itself — the journey is not shortened — so the benefit must be that each stop is reliable and known in advance.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the passage concerns the merchants' earnings; the caravanserai is described as shelter, not as a market.
whyWrong.B: The sentence explicitly says the buildings work "not by shortening it," so this is the option the text rejects.
whyWrong.C: Solitary contradicts the description of merchants who had never met sleeping side by side in a shared courtyard.

tips: When a sentence says "not by X but by _____," the blank must name something other than X — check the choices against the rejected half first.

whyCorrect: The passage sets taste against something else, and the evidence given is medical: the treatment releases niacin the gut can otherwise not absorb, and populations that skipped it got pellagra. The steeping is therefore a matter of what the food does for the body.

whyWrong.B: Convenience concerns ease of preparation, but soaking maize overnight in ash adds work rather than saving it.
whyWrong.C: Storage is never mentioned; the passage tracks what happens to the grain's niacin, not to its shelf life.
whyWrong.D: Ceremony would treat the practice as symbolic, which conflicts with the concrete disease evidence given.

commonMistakes: The detail about the smell tempts students toward a taste- or preparation-related answer, but the sentence rules taste out.

whyCorrect: The sentence before defines the word for you: what comes out of the furnace is "a spongy mass of metal shot through with slag." The underlined word is what the smith then hammers, so it names that object.

whyWrong.A: This is the flower sense of the word, which has no place in a passage about a furnace and a hammer.
whyWrong.C: This is the "boom" or growth sense; nothing here is expanding or prospering.
whyWrong.D: The film-on-a-surface sense exists, but it is a thin coating, not something a smith folds over and strikes.

tips: Underlined-word questions almost always define the word in the neighbouring sentence — find that definition before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank explains it: nothing done in shellac forecloses what a later hand may do. That points back to the earlier detail that the finish "can be lifted again with more alcohol by anyone who wants to begin over." A finish that can be taken off and redone is reversible.

whyWrong.B: Durable would mean it resists removal, which is the opposite of the property the passage praises.
whyWrong.C: Cost is never discussed, and cheapness would not explain why a later hand keeps its options open.
whyWrong.D: Shellac's relationship with water is not mentioned, and being waterproof would say nothing about undoing the work.

tips: A colon after the blank is a definition — read the clause that follows it before looking at the options.

whyCorrect: The colon supplies the test case: someone who had never seen a printed note could join on Monday and sing by Friday. The notation replaces staff positions with shapes precisely so a beginner does not have to learn the staff first. That is speed of learning.

whyWrong.A: Nothing suggests the system was meant to keep outsiders from copying the music; the shapes are printed openly in a tune book.
whyWrong.C: Appearance is beside the point — the shapes carry information about scale degrees, and the passage measures success in how fast a newcomer can sing.
whyWrong.D: Printing costs are never raised, and the sentence contrasts learning with recording new sound, not with expense.

commonMistakes: The blank is explained by the example after the colon, not by the details about the seating square.

whyCorrect: Track the passage's three moves. It opens with something counterintuitive — a bell is cast deliberately too thick and then cut away; it explains the acoustics that make this necessary — five partials whose intervals depend on the wall profile; and it closes with the limitation that follows, that metal cannot be replaced, so tuning runs only from sharp to flat.

whyWrong.A: No individual founder or particular bell is followed; the passage describes the general procedure.
whyWrong.B: Machine tuning versus the ear is never raised, and the lathe is presented as part of the standard method rather than as a replacement for anything.
whyWrong.D: No other instrument's bells appear in the text, so there is no comparison.

tips: For a structure question, summarise each sentence in three or four words and see which choice matches the sequence you get.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence states the point and the rest of the passage backs it up: a sighting ring gives a bearing, a bearing is a line rather than a point, and every acre along that line matches the sighting equally well. Only a second tower's bearing fixes the position. The purpose is to explain why one observation is not enough.

whyWrong.B: The map table appears only as the instrument used; its construction is never described.
whyWrong.C: Aircraft are not mentioned, and the passage makes no recommendation about replacing anything.
whyWrong.D: No dates, places or historical development are given, so the text is not a history.

commonMistakes: A purpose question asks why the text was written; a choice naming a detail the text uses along the way is too narrow.

whyCorrect: The passage says explicitly that what accumulated "was not a library," then lists the trivial items — a bill of lading, an alphabet exercise, a shopping list — and closes by saying the collection is valuable to historians for exactly the reason it was never valuable to its owners. That reason is its ordinariness, which is what choice D states.

whyWrong.A: The text denies this: material was kept because of a religious prohibition on destroying God's name, and the result was explicitly "not a library."
whyWrong.B: Prayer books are named only as one item among many, and the point of the list is how much of the contents is not religious.
whyWrong.C: Commercial value is not why anything survived; the bill of lading was preserved by the same blanket prohibition as the shopping list.

tips: When a passage says what something is not and then gives a list, the main idea usually turns on that list.

whyCorrect: The passage does three things that a main idea has to hold together: the pigment is manufactured, it has a property its makers could not have known about, and that property lets conservators photograph blank stone and recover invisible decoration. Choice C is the only option that keeps all three.

whyWrong.A: The recipe was lost for fifteen centuries, but the passage opens by stating what the pigment is made of, so it is clearly known now.
whyWrong.B: The whole point of the infrared technique is that the traces are invisible, so colour alone cannot identify them.
whyWrong.D: The text says the pigment is manufactured rather than mined; it never claims it was the first such pigment.

commonMistakes: Distractor D adds a superlative the passage never uses — watch for "first," "only" and "most" in main-idea options.

whyCorrect: Oyelaran's claim is that the tree does something about wasps that take the flowers and give no pollen. Evidence for it has to show the tree responding differently to a cheating wasp than to a pollinating one. Figs entered by non-pollinating wasps being dropped before the eggs mature is exactly that: the cheater's offspring die, and the tree is what kills them.

whyWrong.B: Losing her wings is a feature of the wasp's own life cycle and applies to pollinators and cheats alike, so it distinguishes nothing.
whyWrong.C: Staggered flowering times keep species apart; it says nothing about how a tree treats a wasp of its own species that fails to pollinate.
whyWrong.D: A wasp dying in the wrong species' fig is a mistake about which tree to enter, not a penalty imposed on cheating.

tips: Support-the-argument questions want a finding in which the proposed mechanism has a visible effect — here, the tree acting selectively.

whyCorrect: Raman has to rule out the rival explanation that recall simply gives students more exposure to the material. Choice C strips the exposure away entirely: the recall attempts largely failed, and the students never saw the passage again, so they gained almost no additional contact with the content — yet they still beat the rereaders. The advantage must come from the attempt itself.

whyWrong.A: A time saving makes recall more efficient but leaves open whether the benefit came from retrieval or from exposure.
whyWrong.B: Forgetting over a week happens in both groups and says nothing about why one group forgot less.
whyWrong.D: Confidence is a feeling about learning, not a measure of it, and the rereaders' confidence does not address the mechanism at all.

commonMistakes: The strongest support removes the competing cause rather than adding another fact about the winning group.

whyCorrect: Adeyemi sets a pricing motive against a coin-scarcity motive, so the useful finding compares places where the two explanations predict different things. Choice A does: where an independent shop was within reach the company store charged the same, and where it was not the same goods cost a third more. Prices tracking the absence of competition, not the absence of coin, is the pattern his argument predicts.

whyWrong.B: This supports the explanation Adeyemi is arguing against, since genuine scarcity of coin is the convenience story.
whyWrong.C: Extending credit is a separate service and is compatible with either motive.
whyWrong.D: Small denominations would actually help the convenience explanation, and in any case say nothing about prices.

tips: When an argument names a rival explanation, look for the choice that varies one factor and holds the other constant.

whyCorrect: Follow the chain the passage builds: the alga is dark, dark snow absorbs light instead of reflecting it, absorbed light melts snow, and the meltwater carries the nutrients the alga needs to grow. That closes a loop — the bloom speeds the melt, and the melt feeds the bloom. Only choice C states both halves.

whyWrong.A: Snowfall totals are never mentioned, and nothing in the passage links bloom size to how much snow fell.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the physics given: a dark surface takes in light that fresh snow would have reflected, which speeds melting rather than slowing it.
whyWrong.D: Meltwater is what delivers the alga's nutrients, so its appearance promotes growth rather than ending it.

commonMistakes: Choice B is the right topic with the sign flipped — check whether absorbing light warms or cools the surface before choosing.

whyCorrect: The passage says the divergence between the cylinder and its copies was observed, so detection is not the problem. What could not be settled is which side moved, because the cylinder defined the unit and by definition always weighed exactly a kilogram. The blank therefore names assigning the change to a particular object.

whyWrong.B: The drift was measured to within a few tens of micrograms, so accuracy was clearly available.
whyWrong.C: Nothing prevents reporting the discrepancy; the limitation is one of interpretation, not communication.
whyWrong.D: The passage describes weighings repeated over decades, so repeating the observation was not the difficulty.

tips: When a text says something "could be detected but not _____," the blank names the next step the reasoning cannot take.

whyCorrect: "They are tuned to the notes of the tune being played and sound of their own" is one complete sentence, and "the instrument gives the impression that a second fiddle is playing quietly in the next room" is another. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them require a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: A colon is never followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause states a result rather than the explanation a colon would introduce.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation at all the two clauses run together as a fused sentence.

commonMistakes: The "and" earlier in the sentence joins two verbs for the same subject, not two clauses — it does not license a comma later on.

whyCorrect: A dash has already been opened after "slow down" to introduce the list of things that slow — temperature, breathing, heart rate. That list is an interruption, and an interruption opened with a dash has to be closed with a matching dash before the sentence resumes. Choice C supplies the closing dash.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon cannot close a dash, and a semicolon followed by "and" is not standard punctuation between clauses.
whyWrong.B: This leaves the opening dash unclosed and runs the interrupting list straight into the following clause.
whyWrong.D: A comma cannot close a dash; the two marks have to be paired with each other.

tips: Parenthetical punctuation comes in matched pairs — a dash opens, a dash closes; a comma opens, a comma closes.

whyCorrect: The material after the blank is not a second sentence but a relative clause: "which Parliament made the legal standard for the country only forty years afterwards," where "which" refers to the single time the companies imposed. A non-restrictive relative clause attaches to the main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon has to join two independent clauses, and "which Parliament made the legal standard" cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.C: A colon also needs to be followed by material that completes or explains the first clause, not by a relative clause built on "which."
whyWrong.D: A full stop leaves "Which Parliament made the legal standard for the country only forty years afterwards" as a fragment.

commonMistakes: Seeing a long stretch of words after the blank makes it look like a second sentence — check whether it starts with a relative pronoun first.

whyCorrect: "Because" governs everything up to "where it appears to be," including both halves joined by the inner "and," so that whole stretch is a dependent clause. The main clause is "the fish has to correct for the refraction before it fires," and an opening dependent clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause on its left, and the "Because" clause is dependent.
whyWrong.B: A colon has the same requirement, so it cannot follow a "Because" clause.
whyWrong.C: Adding "and" pulls the main clause inside the "Because" clause, leaving the sentence a fragment.

tips: Two independent-looking halves joined by "and" are still dependent if a single "Because" sits in front of them both.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase "Setting the tesserae into the wet plaster," and a phrase like that attaches to whatever noun follows the comma. Whoever is doing the setting has to be that noun, and only the mosaicists can set tesserae. Choice C puts them there as the subject.

whyWrong.A: "The angles" cannot set tesserae into plaster, so the opening phrase dangles.
whyWrong.B: "A slight variation" is the subject, and a variation does not set anything into wet plaster.
whyWrong.D: "There" is an empty subject with no agent at all, leaving the participial phrase with nothing sensible to modify.

tips: When a sentence starts with an -ing phrase, read the word just after the comma and ask whether it can perform that action.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists the scale's purposes, and the first two are infinitives: "to standardise what observers recorded" and "to make one ship's log comparable with another's." The item after "and" is the third in that list, so it has to take the same form. "To produce a single number" keeps the series parallel.

whyWrong.B: "It produces" is a full clause, which breaks the list and leaves "and" joining a clause to two infinitive phrases.
whyWrong.C: "Having produced" is a perfect participle and puts the third purpose in the past relative to the others, which the list does not support.
whyWrong.D: "Producing" is a gerund or participle rather than an infinitive, so the third item no longer matches the first two.

commonMistakes: Check the items before the "and," not just the words nearest the blank — parallelism is decided by the whole list.

whyCorrect: Both events are in the past, and the sentence orders them: "By the time the painter came to work on the border" is the later past moment, and the wearing out of the brush happened before it. English marks the earlier of two past events with the past perfect, so "had worn" is required.

whyWrong.A: "Will wear" is future, which cannot describe something already finished before a past moment.
whyWrong.B: "Is wearing" is present progressive and puts the wearing in the present, contradicting "By the time the painter came."
whyWrong.C: "Wears" is simple present and states a general habit, which does not fit a specific completed sequence in the past.

tips: "By the time" plus a past-tense clause is a reliable signal that the other verb needs the past perfect.

whyCorrect: The first sentence lists two advantages: the store keeps heat for months and it is far cheaper than a battery. The second sentence introduces the limitation — the energy comes back only as heat and will not run a motor or charge a phone. That reverses the positive picture, so the transition has to mark a contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make the limitation follow from the advantages, but cheapness and long storage do not cause the energy to be locked into the form of heat.
whyWrong.B: "Similarly" would mean the second sentence points the same way as the first; it points the opposite way.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would make the second sentence an example of the first, and a restriction is not an example of an advantage.

commonMistakes: A sentence full of praise followed by a real drawback is a contrast, not a consequence.

whyCorrect: You might expect that a language with one word for blue and green would leave its speakers less able to tell the shades apart. The second sentence reports the opposite: they sort the chips with no difficulty. Because the finding runs against what the first sentence sets up, the transition must be concessive.

whyWrong.B: "Consequently" says the sorting ability follows from having a single colour word, which reverses the expected relationship.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" claims the two sentences agree, but the second undercuts the implication of the first.
whyWrong.D: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence adds new experimental evidence rather than condensing what came before.

tips: Ask what the first sentence leads you to expect; if the second sentence disappoints that expectation, the transition is a contrast.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences build a causal chain: grooved hair holds rainwater, algae grow in it, and the sloth is too slow to rub the growth off. The green colour in the third sentence is the outcome of that chain, so the transition marks a result.

whyWrong.A: "In other words" signals a restatement, but the green colour is a new fact rather than a rephrasing of how algae grow.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" needs an opposition, and the green colour agrees with everything said before it.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" would mean the sloth is green despite the algae, which contradicts the mechanism just described.

tips: When two or three sentences build a chain of causes, the sentence after them is almost always the effect.

whyCorrect: To show the distortion was deliberate you need the design decision and the cost Beck knowingly paid for it. Choice A joins them: he straightened every line to one of three directions, and he accepted that distances would no longer correspond to distances on the ground. The word "accepting" is what marks the distortion as a choice rather than a mistake.

whyWrong.B: The publicity department's rejection shows the design was controversial, not that its distortion was intentional.
whyWrong.C: Strong sales show the map worked for passengers but say nothing about Beck's intentions.
whyWrong.D: The date and the fact that he worked in his own time are background and mention no distortion at all.

commonMistakes: A note that proves the map was successful is not the same as one that proves the distortion was on purpose.

whyCorrect: Forgery means producing a matching half that is not genuine. The two notes that make that hard are the splitting of each stick with the halves held by different parties, and the fact that a split stick's grain matches only its own partner. Choice D is the only option that uses either of them.

whyWrong.A: The 1834 fire is the end of the system's history and has nothing to do with security.
whyWrong.B: The length of time the method was used shows it was durable, not that it resisted forgery.
whyWrong.C: Circulation as credit explains what tallies were used for, which is a different question from why they were hard to fake.

tips: Match the choice to the goal's key word — here "forge" points to verification, so look for the note about matching.

whyCorrect: The goal has two sides, the pillar and modern iron, so the sentence needs the mechanism for one and the reason it is absent from the other. Choice A gives both: the high phosphorus produces a sealing film of iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate, and modern iron has the phosphorus removed because it makes steel brittle.

whyWrong.B: This states the fact to be explained rather than explaining it.
whyWrong.C: This covers modern iron only and never mentions the protective film, so it explains nothing about the pillar.
whyWrong.D: The date and height are descriptive background with no bearing on corrosion.

commonMistakes: When a goal contains a comparison, a choice describing only one side of it cannot meet the goal.

whyCorrect: Everything described is transport of a liquid: the belly feathers take up water like a wick, hold it over fifty kilometres, and give it up when the chicks draw the feathers through their beaks. The blank has to name something that carries and holds water, and the sentence contrasts that role with insulation, which is what belly plumage normally does.

whyWrong.B: A shield protects against something, but the feathers are described as taking water in rather than keeping anything out.
whyWrong.C: Decoration would be about appearance, and no display or colour is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
whyWrong.D: A signal communicates information to another animal; the chicks drink from the feathers rather than read them.

tips: When the sentence says "best understood as X rather than as Y," X has to name the function the passage just demonstrated.

whyCorrect: The colon defines the blank: any fixed line leading away from the dung pile will serve. The beetle is not heading anywhere in particular, it just needs a constant direction to keep, which is what it reads off the Milky Way. A bearing is precisely a direction rather than a place.

whyWrong.A: Shelter is a place of safety, and the beetle is rolling away from the pile rather than looking for cover.
whyWrong.B: A companion is another animal; the beetle takes its reading from the sky and travels alone.
whyWrong.D: A landmark is a fixed point on the ground, and the passage stresses that the beetle uses a line rather than a destination — and takes it from the sky in the dark.

commonMistakes: "Landmark" is close enough to navigation to feel right; the sentence rules it out by contrasting a direction with a destination.

whyCorrect: The passage says outright that the reading changed nothing about the flood itself, and then lists what it did change: the tax to be demanded and the amount of grain the granaries held back. Those are decisions of government and record-keeping, so the instrument's real function was administrative.

whyWrong.A: Experimental would mean the readings tested something about the river, and the text says explicitly that they changed nothing about the flood.
whyWrong.B: Nothing is measured against the sky; the shaft reads the water level in the river.
whyWrong.D: Ornamental would make the shaft decorative, but every use given for it is practical.

tips: "Less a scientific device than an _____ one" tells you the answer must name the non-scientific use the passage has just listed.

whyCorrect: The cold is made outside the building, by water radiating heat to the clear night sky. The building's contribution is the deep pit, the metre-thick walls and the vent that keep the ice frozen into high summer. So the blank names holding on to cold that already exists, which is what the preceding sentence sets it against.

whyWrong.A: Circulating cold would mean moving it about, and the vent at the apex is described as helping to hold the ice, not to distribute it.
whyWrong.B: Produce is the verb the previous sentence rules out — the building "does not make cold."
whyWrong.C: Predicting has nothing to do with the structure; nothing in the passage forecasts anything.

commonMistakes: The two sentences are a set-up and a payoff — the blank must contradict "make," not repeat it in different words.

whyCorrect: The passage is explicit that the barbules carry no unusual pigment, so the blackness cannot come from a substance. What it comes from is shape: a forest of curved spikes that traps a ray and bounces it until it is absorbed. The blank must name that geometric cause, in contrast with a chemical one.

whyWrong.A: Inherited describes how the trait passes between generations and is not an alternative to a chemical explanation.
whyWrong.C: Seasonal implies the blackness comes and goes with the year, which the text never suggests.
whyWrong.D: Accidental conflicts with a highly specific arrangement of curved spikes that functions as a light trap.

tips: The word before "rather than" fixes the axis of contrast — chemical here, so the answer must be a non-chemical mechanism.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence separates two things that are easy to confuse: a limit on cargo and a limit on how deep the hull may sit. Everything after it develops exactly that distinction — the same ship may load to the line in one sea and must stop short in another, so the permitted tonnage changes with the voyage while the depth limit does not.

whyWrong.A: No painting procedure is described; the sentence is about what the mark means, not how it is applied.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the passage says owners ignored the mark, so there is no concession to make.
whyWrong.D: Timber is never mentioned, and the passage draws no distinction between kinds of cargo.

tips: If a sentence says "not X but Y," check whether the following sentences work out the consequences of Y — that is usually its function.

whyCorrect: Most of the text describes the allotment machine in physical detail — the slots, the tickets, the tube of black and white balls, the crank. The last two sentences then narrow its purpose: it settled nothing about who was fit to judge, only that no official had chosen them. Describing the mechanism and naming that one narrow question is what the text does.

whyWrong.B: No comparison with modern juries is made, and the text explicitly declines to say anything about the quality of the jurors.
whyWrong.C: No period of development is traced; the passage describes a single device in operation.
whyWrong.D: The tickets appear only as objects pushed into the slots, with nothing said about how they were made or inscribed.

commonMistakes: The closing sentences look like a limitation, but stating what a device does not decide is part of identifying what it does decide.

whyCorrect: The passage establishes the city's size, then reports the absence of a siege line, a mass grave or a burnt layer — the evidence you would expect from a violent end. The closing description is of a city that drew people in and let them go again across decades. Both halves together give a large city that emptied slowly.

whyWrong.A: The text lists the missing traces of war precisely to rule this explanation out.
whyWrong.C: The mound is compared with the Great Pyramid in area only; the text never claims it is the largest earthwork anywhere.
whyWrong.D: The passage says people were drawn in from several regions, not from the flood plain alone.

tips: When a passage inventories evidence that is absent, it is usually eliminating a rival explanation — check whether a choice is the one being eliminated.

whyCorrect: The experiment works by sight alone: the mirror puts a reflection of the intact hand where the missing one used to be, and the patient watches the missing hand open. The reported outcome is that the cramp eased for some and stayed away for a few. The main idea has to pair the visual illusion with that partial relief.

whyWrong.A: There is no limb left to restore feeling to; what changes is what the patient sees, not the amputated arm.
whyWrong.C: The passage offers no account of what causes phantom pain, and nerve endings are never mentioned.
whyWrong.D: The text is careful about scope — relief came "for some" and lasted "for a few" — so a claim about every patient overstates it.

commonMistakes: Choice D is the passage's result with its qualifiers stripped out; main-idea answers must keep the hedges the text uses.

whyCorrect: Duarte's claim is that foot survey missed settlement because it could only record cleared ground. The finding that supports her has to show structures in exactly the places foot survey wrote off. House platforms, causeways and field walls turning up across areas previously recorded as empty forest is that finding, and it is what makes the old population figures too low.

whyWrong.A: Large pyramids stand above the canopy and were always visible, so mapping them confirms nothing about what the ground survey missed.
whyWrong.B: This is a limitation of the laser method and, if anything, works against the new survey's completeness.
whyWrong.C: The date of abandonment concerns when the cities ended, not how many people lived in them.

tips: Support questions reward the finding that fills the specific gap the argument identifies — here, settlement under unbroken forest.

whyCorrect: Teo claims dependence, which means these trees fail to disperse where the cassowary is gone. Choice B tests exactly that: seedlings appear away from a parent tree only in forest where cassowaries still range, and nowhere else. That is the comparison that turns "the bird eats the fruit" into "the tree cannot manage without the bird."

whyWrong.A: A varied cassowary diet describes the bird's needs, not the tree's reliance on it.
whyWrong.C: Falling cassowary numbers establish that the risk is real but leave open whether these trees actually depend on the bird for dispersal.
whyWrong.D: Bright colour suggests the fruit attracts an animal but does not show that only the cassowary disperses it.

commonMistakes: A finding about the threatened species and a finding about the dependence are different claims; the argument here needs the dependence.

whyCorrect: Moretti sets collection labour against a trade secret held in Tyre. If the secret mattered, dye made elsewhere would be inferior or cheaper. Choice D reports the opposite: workshops far from Tyre matched the quality as soon as they had snails, and charged as much — so the cost tracked the snails, not any proprietary knowledge.

whyWrong.A: Sumptuary law restricted who could wear the colour, which affects demand rather than the source of the cost.
whyWrong.B: The chemistry going unexplained until the twentieth century says nothing about whether ancient dyers guarded a technique.
whyWrong.C: The stench explains where dyeworks were sited and is unrelated to why the dye cost what it did.

tips: When an argument names two rival causes, look for the choice in which one cause is removed and the outcome stays the same.

whyCorrect: The passage eliminates the alternatives for you: no residue rules out glue, and gripping inside a vacuum rules out suction. What is left in the description is the geometry — half a million hairs, each split into hundreds of finer tips, which lets the foot touch the surface at an enormous number of points. An attraction that arises simply from that closeness of contact is what remains.

whyWrong.A: The gecko hangs from polished glass, so roughness cannot be what the grip depends on.
whyWrong.C: Air pressure is suction by another name, and the grip works in a vacuum where there is no air to press.
whyWrong.D: A secreted fluid is the glue explanation, which the absence of any residue rules out.

tips: When a text rules options out one by one, the blank is whatever survives the eliminations — check each choice against them.

whyCorrect: The passage draws the contrast directly: the caesium interval does not vary, while tides, atmospheric movement and post-glacial rebound change the length of a day. Extra seconds have to be inserted at unpredictable intervals because the thing being tracked wanders, and that thing is the Earth's rotation.

whyWrong.A: The text says the caesium interval "does not vary," which is the fixed standard the comparison is made against.
whyWrong.C: Tides are only one of three causes the passage lists, so "and nothing else" contradicts the text.
whyWrong.D: Nothing suggests the clocks are unreliable; their steadiness is what makes the Earth's variation visible.

commonMistakes: Choice C is right in substance but wrong in scope — the "nothing else" is what makes it false.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is "Kilwa," and "a town whose merchants handled the gold carried up from the Zimbabwe plateau" is an appositive describing it. An appositive opened with a comma has to be closed with one before the verb, giving "Kilwa, a town …, had a palace."

whyWrong.B: A semicolon would need an independent clause on each side, and "had a palace of more than a hundred rooms" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.C: A colon also requires a complete clause before it, and the sentence so far is only a subject plus an unfinished appositive.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the appositive never closes, so the subject runs straight into the verb.

tips: An appositive is punctuated in pairs — if you can see the opening comma, the blank almost certainly needs the closing one.

whyCorrect: "Two separate things are responsible for the difference" is a complete clause that announces a list, and what follows is that list — the ellipse of the orbit and the tilt of the axis. A colon is the mark that introduces a list after a complete clause.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but the material after the blank is a pair of noun phrases, not a sentence.
whyWrong.C: "And" plus a comma would attach the ellipse as a coordinate element, leaving the promised list ungoverned and the sentence incoherent.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the list runs into the clause that introduces it.

tips: A clause that says how many things are coming — "two separate things" — is almost always followed by a colon.

whyCorrect: The subject is "Michael Thonet," and "a cabinetmaker who patented the process in the 1850s and sold his chairs by the million" is an appositive describing him. It opened with a comma after his name, so it has to close with a comma before the main verb "shipped."

whyWrong.A: Without the closing comma the appositive is left open and "shipped" has no clear subject.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs a complete clause on each side, and "shipped the rods and screws unassembled" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon likewise requires an independent clause before it, which a subject plus an unfinished appositive is not.

commonMistakes: The appositive here is long enough that students forget it started with a comma — find the opening mark before choosing.

whyCorrect: "Jacquard's mechanism replaced him with three things" is a complete clause, and everything after the blank is the list of those three things — the loop of cards, the row of hooks and the cylinder. A colon after a complete clause is what introduces such a list.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the list runs straight into the clause and the reader has no signal that an enumeration has begun.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and "a loop of stiff cards punched with holes" is a noun phrase.
whyWrong.D: "And" would make the loop the last item of a list rather than the first, and the two remaining items would then have nowhere to attach.

tips: "Three things," "two reasons," "the following" — a counted announcement takes a colon before the items.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The collection," which is singular. "Along with the notebooks that go with it" is a parenthetical phrase, and a phrase introduced by along with, as well as or in addition to never changes the number of the subject. The sentence also describes present practice, so the singular present "is" is required.

whyWrong.A: "Have been" is plural and would need a plural subject such as the notebooks, which are inside the parenthetical phrase.
whyWrong.B: "Were" is both plural and past, so it fails the agreement and contradicts "today."
whyWrong.D: "Are" is plural; it agrees with "notebooks" rather than with the actual subject, "collection."

tips: Cross out any phrase between commas before choosing a verb — the subject is what remains.

whyCorrect: The subject is "Each," not "panels." "Each" is always singular, and "of the eleven panels recovered from the site" is a prepositional phrase that cannot supply the subject. The singular present verb is "shows."

whyWrong.A: "Show" is the plural form and agrees with "panels," which sits inside a prepositional phrase.
whyWrong.C: "Showing" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb and would be a fragment.
whyWrong.D: "Were showing" is plural and past progressive, wrong in number and wrong for a statement about what the surviving panels still display.

commonMistakes: A plural noun just before the verb pulls students toward a plural verb; with "each of," the verb is always singular.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between two capacities: the one measured in the geese and the one measured in lowland species. English uses "that" to stand in for a singular noun in this kind of comparison, and "capacity" is singular. "Higher than that measured in the blood of related lowland species" is the correct form.

whyWrong.A: "Them" is an object pronoun and would refer to the geese, producing a comparison between a capacity and a group of birds.
whyWrong.B: "Which" would start a relative clause needing its own verb, and "which measured in the blood" has none.
whyWrong.C: "Those" is plural and would need a plural noun to stand for; the noun being compared, "capacity," is singular.

tips: In comparisons, "that" replaces a singular noun and "those" a plural one — check what is actually being compared.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the old system — recipient pays, price by distance and sheets, refusals costing the Post Office. The second describes Hill's system, which reverses every one of those features: sender pays, price by weight, no refusals. The transition must mark that the two systems are being set against each other.

whyWrong.A: "Moreover" adds a further point in the same direction, but the second sentence replaces the arrangement rather than extending it.
whyWrong.B: "Nonetheless" would say the penny post held despite the old system, which is not a concession the sentences support.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" would make the penny post an example of the pre-1840 arrangement, when it is its replacement.

tips: When the second sentence reverses each feature named in the first, the transition marks contrast.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences report the experiment and the fact that knowing about the illusion does not remove it. The third does not add evidence; it states what those facts amount to — that awareness receives a settlement between the two channels rather than either channel itself. That is a restatement at a higher level, so the transition signals rephrasing.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" needs the third sentence to run against the first two, but it agrees with them and explains them.
whyWrong.B: "For instance" would make the third sentence a further example, and it introduces no new case.
whyWrong.C: "Meanwhile" marks something happening at the same time elsewhere, which does not describe an interpretive summary.

commonMistakes: A sentence that names the upshot of the evidence is a restatement, not a new example.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim: different silks for different jobs. The second gives two particular silks and the particular jobs they do — the stiff dragline and the stretchy capture spiral. That is an illustration of the general claim, so the transition introduces an example.

whyWrong.A: "By contrast" would set the second sentence against the first, but the dragline and spiral illustrate the first rather than oppose it. The contrast inside the sentence is handled by "while."
whyWrong.B: "Consequently" claims the properties of the two silks follow from the general statement, when they are instances of it.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" signals a concession, and nothing in the second sentence works against the first.

tips: A general claim followed by named particulars is an example, even when those particulars are contrasted with each other.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why growers came to depend on bumblebees, which needs three things: what the bumblebee does, why no other managed bee will do it, and what growers did before. Choice D carries all three — the vibration that frees the pollen, the honeybee's inability to produce it, and the switch from hand pollination once colonies were sold.

whyWrong.A: The pore at the anther tip is background about the flower and does not mention bees at all.
whyWrong.B: The honeybee's limitation is half the answer, but on its own it never says what the bumblebee does or that growers took it up.
whyWrong.C: The availability of colonies gives the date without the reason growers needed them.

tips: A goal phrased as "why X came to depend on Y" usually needs both the capability and the absence of an alternative.

whyCorrect: "Survives without recovering" has two halves, and choice C is the only option with both. The root system living on and sending up shoots is the survival; the shoots dying before they can set seed is why there is no recovery — no seed means no new generation of mature trees.

whyWrong.A: The species' former abundance is background and describes neither survival nor its limits.
whyWrong.B: The scale of the die-off explains the loss but says nothing about anything that survived it.
whyWrong.D: The breeding programme is an attempt at recovery in the future, not an account of the present situation.

commonMistakes: When a goal joins two ideas with "without," a choice covering only one of them cannot satisfy it.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for a reason, so the sentence has to connect the music to the instrument. Choice A does: the studies layer tempo ratios such as 17:18 that no two performers can hold together, so he wrote for a machine that reads punched holes. That is a cause followed by its consequence.

whyWrong.B: How rarely the studies were heard is a fact about their reception, not a reason for the choice of instrument.
whyWrong.C: Describing how a player piano works explains the machine but never says why Nancarrow needed it.
whyWrong.D: The date and the hand-punching describe his working method rather than his motive.

tips: For a "why" goal, check that the chosen sentence actually contains a because-relationship, not just two related facts.

whyCorrect: The clause before the blank says nothing in the empty air marks where one note ends and the next begins, and the clause after it says every pitch has to be found by ear. What the player is missing is a physical reference point of the kind a fret or a key provides. "Landmarks" names exactly that.

whyWrong.B: Amplification concerns loudness, and the passage says the hands control volume as well as pitch, so nothing is lacking there.
whyWrong.C: Resonance is a property of the sound produced, not a guide to where a note lies.
whyWrong.D: Notation is written music, which is external to any instrument and would not help a player locate a pitch in mid-air.

tips: Read the clause after the blank first — "found by ear alone" tells you the missing thing is a physical guide.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets "continuous" against the blank, so the blank must name something the practice is not, despite being unbroken. The passage says a wall is repainted every season and the painter alters the design rather than copying it. The tradition persists while its designs keep changing, so it is continuous without being fixed.

whyWrong.A: The painting plainly is decorative, so this would contradict the passage rather than complete the contrast.
whyWrong.B: The designs are on outer walls and could hardly be more visible.
whyWrong.C: Nothing suggests the practice is not shared; the passage describes it as what Ndebele women do generally.

commonMistakes: In an "X without being Y" frame, Y must be something the passage denies — check each option against what the text actually says.

whyCorrect: The mechanism given is storage in separate chambers, with the two chemicals kept apart until the beetle is threatened and they meet over a catalyst. The final clause explains why: mixed early, the reaction would destroy the beetle. The blank therefore names being kept separate.

whyWrong.A: Dilution is never mentioned, and weakening the reagents would not prevent them reacting once combined.
whyWrong.C: Chilling is not described anywhere; the temperature that matters is the boiling-hot spray at the moment of firing.
whyWrong.D: Concentration says nothing about keeping the two chemicals from meeting, which is the danger the sentence identifies.

tips: When a passage describes separate chambers and a moment of mixing, the blank is about separation, not about the chemicals' state.

whyCorrect: The reasoning runs: the grain of a stick is unique, the two halves fit each other and nothing else, and a forged half would fail the simplest test. The "Since" clause makes the blank the conclusion drawn from that, so it has to name resistance to faking.

whyWrong.A: A stick is portable, but portability has nothing to do with a forged half failing a test, which is the reason given.
whyWrong.B: Hazel sticks are cheap, and cost is not raised anywhere in the passage.
whyWrong.D: The system is explicitly medieval English practice, and modernity is not a conclusion the forgery test supports.

tips: When the sentence opens with "Since" plus a reason, the blank must be what that reason proves.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes what is put on the plate: a thin acid-resistant coating of wax and resin. The underlined word then names what the needle clears away and where the acid can bite, so it refers back to that coating.

whyWrong.A: The figure-and-background sense belongs to painting and does not fit a substance a needle removes.
whyWrong.B: The earth sense is the everyday one, but no soil or land appears in a passage about a copper plate and an acid bath.
whyWrong.D: The "reason offered in support" sense is abstract and cannot be cleared away by a needle.

commonMistakes: The most familiar meaning of a word is rarely the one being tested — work from the sentence that describes what the thing does.

whyCorrect: Follow the four sentences. The first states the limitation — a drawing does not move. The next describes the drum that seems to defeat it. The third and fourth explain that the gaps are what matter and that the device supplies not motion but the interruption that lets stills read as motion. Statement, apparent solution, actual contribution.

whyWrong.A: Motion-picture cameras are never mentioned, so there is no comparison to be made.
whyWrong.B: No inventor, date or patent appears; the text explains how the device works, not how it came about.
whyWrong.C: The eye is discussed only as what sees through the slots, and the passage makes no argument about how easily it is fooled.

tips: Structure questions are answered by summarising each sentence in turn and matching the sequence, not by finding a familiar-sounding topic.

whyCorrect: The final sentence says searches for a conductor have failed because there is nothing of the kind to find. That claim only stands if synchrony can arise without a leader, and the underlined sentence is what shows it can: each insect adjusts its own cycle towards its neighbours, and a population doing only that settles into a common beat. It supplies the mechanism the conclusion rests on.

whyWrong.A: The sentence affirms that a common beat emerges; it does not doubt that the flashing is synchronised.
whyWrong.B: The habitat — bankside trees along Thai rivers — is given in the first sentence, not the underlined one.
whyWrong.C: The failed search is reported in the last sentence; the underlined sentence explains why that search was bound to fail.

tips: When the last sentence gives a "because" with no support of its own, look back for the sentence that supplies it.

whyCorrect: The passage says local time was tolerable at the speed of a horse and not on a railway, then gives the reason: two trains sharing one track are separated by a timetable, and a timetable is worthless if the crews are working to different clocks. That is the specific failure the question asks about.

whyWrong.A: No disagreement among astronomers is mentioned; each town's noon was a straightforward local observation.
whyWrong.B: Resetting watches is described as something travellers did, and the passage treats it as tolerable rather than as what broke the system.
whyWrong.D: The text says the railway companies imposed the zones and that the law followed thirty-five years later, so the government did not require the standard in 1883.

commonMistakes: Choice B names a real inconvenience from the text; the question asks what made the arrangement unworkable, and the passage says that was a safety problem, not an annoyance.

whyCorrect: The last sentence states the advantage in so many words: the floats do not measure more accurately than a ship, they measure where no ship goes. The sentence before it says ship data came from shipping lanes, in summer, in the northern hemisphere — so the gain is coverage in place and in season.

whyWrong.B: Cost is never mentioned anywhere in the passage.
whyWrong.C: The floats rise only to radio a profile and then sink again, so they do not stay at the surface.
whyWrong.D: The text denies this directly: the floats "do not measure more accurately than a ship does."

tips: When a passage explicitly denies one advantage and asserts another, the denied one is nearly always among the choices.

whyCorrect: If the grove is one individual multiplied by basal shoots, every tree in it is a clone and they should be genetically identical. Sequencing trees from every part of the grove and finding no detectable variation is the direct test of that, because sexual reproduction from seed would leave differences between individuals.

whyWrong.A: Fossil pollen across Australia and Antarctica speaks to the genus's ancient range, not to how the surviving trees are related to one another.
whyWrong.B: Shelter from fire explains why the grove survived and says nothing about whether it is one plant or many.
whyWrong.D: Male and female cones on one plant describe the species' reproductive anatomy; they do not show that the grove is a single clone.

tips: A claim about clonal identity is tested with genetics — look for the choice that compares individuals rather than describing the species.

whyCorrect: Suction needs surrounding air to be excluded from beneath the pad; without air there is no pressure difference to hold the foot on. Adhesion that is just as strong in a near-vacuum therefore cannot be suction, while van der Waals attraction between the hair tips and the surface works regardless of air. That is why choice B favours Boateng over the alternative.

whyWrong.A: Adhesive hairs on other animals show the design is widespread but do not distinguish between the two mechanisms.
whyWrong.C: Peeling tip first describes how the foot is released, which is compatible with either explanation.
whyWrong.D: Better adhesion on smooth surfaces is what both mechanisms predict, since suction and close molecular contact both need a good seal or fit.

commonMistakes: The question asks for support over a named alternative, so the finding must be one the alternative cannot accommodate.

whyCorrect: Corrigan claims the two pore types are combined rather than used singly. Choice D tests exactly that by presenting the signals separately and together: the platypus strikes accurately only when the electrical and pressure cues arrive at once, and misses when either is given alone. Failure on each cue by itself is what rules out reliance on either alone.

whyWrong.A: Where the electrical pores sit on the bill is anatomy; it does not show the two senses being used together.
whyWrong.B: Shrimp generating detectable fields shows the electrical sense is usable on its own, which if anything supports the rival account.
whyWrong.C: Nocturnal foraging explains why vision is unhelpful but says nothing about how the two pore types interact.

tips: A claim about two things working together needs an experiment in which each is also tested alone.

whyCorrect: The passage says two effects push solar noon as much as sixteen minutes from clock noon at some times of year and bring the two together at others. "Bring together at others" means the offset passes through zero, and since it varies continuously through the year that happens only on the handful of dates where it crosses. So the two instruments agree on only a few dates.

whyWrong.A: The offset is described as varying through the year, not as vanishing for a whole season; both effects are active in summer as well.
whyWrong.B: Latitude is never mentioned, and neither the elliptical orbit nor the axial tilt is a function of being at the equator.
whyWrong.C: Alignment fixes where the dial points; it cannot remove a discrepancy that changes size and sign through the year.

commonMistakes: "Once correctly aligned" sounds like a fix, but the passage locates the discrepancy in the Earth's motion, which no adjustment to the dial can cancel.

whyCorrect: The passage says which trips stop depends on what alternatives exist, and contrasts a driver with a frequent train against one setting out at four in the morning from an outer suburb. If nothing is done to improve alternatives, the driver with no substitute either pays the charge or gives up a trip they cannot replace. The burden lands on those with the fewest other options.

whyWrong.B: City-centre residents are not discussed, and the charge applies to driving into the centre rather than to living there.
whyWrong.C: Commercial deliveries are never mentioned, and the passage frames the charge around peak-hour commuting.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the drivers who stop coming valued the trip at less than the charge, so the most valuable trips are the ones that continue.

tips: When a passage builds a contrast between two example cases, the blank usually generalises the worse-off case.

whyCorrect: "Because" makes everything up to "inside its host" a dependent clause, and the main clause is "botanists working in Sumatra map the vines rather than the flowers." A dependent clause that opens a sentence is followed by a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and the "Because" clause is dependent.
whyWrong.B: A colon likewise requires a complete clause before it, which the "Because" clause is not.
