whyWrong.C: "And" folds the main clause into the "Because" clause, leaving the sentence with no independent clause at all.

tips: If deleting the opening "Because" would give you two sentences, you are looking at a dependent clause plus a main clause — comma, not semicolon.

whyCorrect: What follows the blank is a relative clause — "which takes up the whole pattern in a single contact and cannot be laid down twice" — describing the sheet of paper. It cannot stand as a sentence, and a non-restrictive relative clause is attached with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and a clause beginning with "which" is not independent.
whyWrong.B: A colon has the same requirement and would also promise an explanation or list rather than a description of the paper.
whyWrong.C: A full stop turns "Which takes up the whole pattern…" into a fragment.

commonMistakes: A long stretch after the blank tempts students toward a semicolon; check the first word — "which" almost always means a comma.

whyCorrect: "John Roebling's mill at Trenton twisted fine wires into strands and the strands into rope" is a complete sentence, and "a rope so made bends around a sheave, and a broken wire inside it can be found and replaced without taking the whole thing down" is another. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them take a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: Repeating "rope" with no punctuation fuses the two independent clauses.
whyWrong.B: A colon cannot be followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause states properties rather than explaining the first.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice; the "and" later in the sentence joins the two halves of the second clause, not the two clauses.

tips: Locate every independent clause first — the "and" you can see may belong to a clause other than the one at the blank.

whyCorrect: "The liquid pours like any other with no magnet near it" is a complete sentence, and "a field held beneath the dish draws the surface up into a bed of spikes" is another. When "but" joins two independent clauses, the comma goes before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: A colon cannot be followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause contrasts with the first rather than explaining it.
whyWrong.B: With no comma the two independent clauses joined by "but" are run together.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon plus "but" doubles the join; the semicolon already does the work the conjunction is doing.

tips: Comma before a coordinating conjunction, semicolon instead of one — never both.

whyCorrect: The subject is "Each," which is singular, and "of the seven seismographs on the flank" is a prepositional phrase that cannot be the subject. A singular subject in the present tense takes "has."

whyWrong.A: "Have" is plural and agrees with "seismographs," which sits inside a prepositional phrase.
whyWrong.C: "Having" is a participle rather than a finite verb, leaving the sentence without a main verb.
whyWrong.D: "Were having" is plural and past progressive, wrong in number and wrong for a standing description of how each station is equipped.

tips: "Each of," "either of" and "neither of" are singular no matter how plural the noun after "of" is.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between two quantities of rainfall — the amount at the upland gauge and the amount at the town gauge. "Rainfall" is singular, and the pronoun standing in for a singular noun in a comparison is "that."

whyWrong.B: "Those" is plural and has no plural noun to refer to; the noun being compared is the singular "rainfall."
whyWrong.C: "Them" is an object pronoun and would point to the gauges, comparing an amount of rain with two instruments.
whyWrong.D: "Which" opens a relative clause that would need its own verb, and "which recorded at the gauge" has none.

commonMistakes: The plural "gauges" earlier in the passage pulls students toward "those"; the comparison is between rainfall amounts, not gauges.

whyCorrect: The relative clause modifies "the few chalk streams," not "this brook" — there are several such streams and the brook is one of them. A plural antecedent takes the plural auxiliary, giving "streams that have never been dredged or realigned."

whyWrong.A: "Is never been dredged" is not a possible verb form.
whyWrong.B: "Has" would be right only if the clause described the single brook, but "one of the few streams that…" makes the clause describe the group.
whyWrong.D: "Having never been dredged" is a participle, so the relative clause would lack a finite verb.

tips: In "one of the few X that …," ask how many things the clause is true of — usually all of the X, so the verb is plural.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the facts: scores rose everywhere, and the tests were periodically made harder so the average would return to a hundred. The second sentence draws out what those facts mean — the score is fixed by comparison with the current population, not against a fixed standard. That is a restatement of the same point in plainer terms.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" requires the second sentence to cut against the first, and it agrees with it.
whyWrong.B: "For instance" would introduce a particular case, but the second sentence is more general than the first, not less.
whyWrong.C: "Meanwhile" marks a simultaneous but separate development, and no second development is described.

tips: If the second sentence tells you what the first sentence amounts to, the transition is a restatement.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes regenerative braking as an efficient way of slowing the car, which sets up the expectation that friction brakes might be dispensed with. The second sentence says they are still fitted, and gives the reason. Since the second reverses what the first leads you to expect, the transition is concessive.

whyWrong.B: "Consequently" would make the friction brakes a result of regenerative braking, but the sentence explains why regeneration is not enough.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" claims agreement between the two sentences, and the second qualifies the first.
whyWrong.D: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence adds a new limitation rather than condensing what came before.

commonMistakes: The "because" clause inside the second sentence supplies its own reason — do not mistake that for a causal link to the first sentence.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes that the hand vocabulary is fixed and carries the same meaning for any audience that knows the form. The second sentence draws the practical consequence: someone too far back to read the dancer's face can still follow the passage. Cause first, effect second.

whyWrong.A: "Similarly" would present the second sentence as a parallel case, but it is a result of the fact just stated.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" needs an opposition, and the second sentence agrees with the first.
whyWrong.D: "Even so" concedes something despite the first sentence, whereas the second follows straightforwardly from it.

tips: Ask whether the second sentence would still be true if the first were false; if not, the link is causal.

whyCorrect: The goal is an obstacle, and the only note describing one is the shared bus fleet, which ties the primary and secondary timetables together so neither can move freely. Choice B uses it, and by setting it against the Minneapolis benefits it makes clear that the obstacle stands even where the change worked.

whyWrong.A: Rising attendance is a benefit of the change, the opposite of an obstacle.
whyWrong.C: An extra hour of sleep is also a result in favour of changing start times.
whyWrong.D: The biological shift at puberty is the reason for wanting a later start, not something standing in its way.

tips: When the goal names an obstacle, scan the notes for the one that describes a constraint rather than a result.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why gathering is limited to certain times of year, and only one note gives a seasonal reason: the bark will lift from the trunk only in the wet season. Choice B states that condition and links it to when sheets are cut.

whyWrong.A: Museum cataloguing and re-attribution concern how the finished paintings were treated, not when material can be collected.
whyWrong.C: Warming and flattening describe what happens to a sheet after it is cut and impose no seasonal limit.
whyWrong.D: The pigments and binder are a separate material with nothing said about their timing.

commonMistakes: Three of the notes are true and about the same practice; only the one containing a seasonal condition can answer a "why only at certain times" goal.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how one singer produces two lines, which needs the mechanism rather than the effect. Choice C supplies it: the melody is not a second note at all but a harmonic already contained in the drone, amplified one at a time by changes in the shape of the mouth and tongue.

whyWrong.A: This states that two lines are heard, which is the thing to be explained.
whyWrong.B: This restates the puzzle even more directly — two voices from one note — without explaining it.
whyWrong.D: Identifying the drone as a single note produced at the vocal folds covers only one of the two lines and says nothing about where the melody comes from.

tips: For a "how" goal, reject any choice that merely reports the phenomenon; you need the sentence containing the mechanism.

whyCorrect: The paper is folded once and cut through both halves in a single stroke, so the two sides cannot come out different — the symmetry follows automatically from the way the cut is made. The sentence contrasts that with being drawn or measured, so the blank names something the method secures without the maker having to aim for it.

whyWrong.A: Sacrificed would mean the symmetry is lost, but the passage says the finished figure is identical on either side of the fold.
whyWrong.B: Hidden makes no sense of a result that is plainly visible in the finished cockerel or spruce.
whyWrong.C: Imitated would suggest an approximation of symmetry, whereas cutting through both halves at once produces the real thing.

tips: When a sentence says a result is "neither drawn nor measured," the blank names how it arises without deliberate effort.

whyCorrect: The passage says the children arrived with no language in common, and that the youngest pupils produced a grammar more regular than anything the first cohort had. Since the sentence explicitly denies that the language was taught, the blank has to describe something coming into being among the children themselves.

whyWrong.B: Survived implies the language already existed and persisted, but the children began with no shared language at all.
whyWrong.C: Declined contradicts the description of increasingly fluent and more regular signing.
whyWrong.D: Spread describes an existing language reaching new users, which again presupposes something that was not there to begin with.

commonMistakes: "Spread" feels close because the younger children learned from the older ones, but the sentence is about where the language came from, not how it circulated.

whyCorrect: The passage first describes ranks of pipes, each with a timbre of its own, and then the knob that admits wind to a rank. "Sixty such" refers back to that pairing, so the underlined word names the rank together with the control that brings it into play — which is why drawing several at once blends their voices.

whyWrong.A: The transport sense of the word has nothing to do with an organ.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the passage puts an obstruction inside a pipe; wind is admitted or withheld at the knob.
whyWrong.D: The "pause in an activity" sense cannot be counted as sixty items in an instrument's layout.

tips: Count what the phrase "sixty such" is counting — that tells you which noun the underlined word is standing for.

whyCorrect: Every later distance was computed from the one baseline, so an error in it would have run through the whole network. That makes the accuracy of everything downstream depend entirely on that single measurement, which is exactly why it was remeasured again and again. "Contingent on" names that dependence.

whyWrong.B: Improved would mean the later work made the measurement better, which reverses the direction of influence the passage describes.
whyWrong.C: Reported concerns how the figure was communicated, and nothing in the sentence is about publication.
whyWrong.D: Irrelevant contradicts the whole passage, including the repeated remeasurement it is offered to explain.

tips: The clause after the comma — "which is why the baseline was remeasured again and again" — has to make sense with your choice in place.

whyCorrect: The passage says the ground was dry until rising seas closed over a plain about eight thousand years ago, and that the nets bring up peat, freshwater shells and worked flint. The sentence rejects the idea that this material washed out from the shore, so the blank must say the landscape is still in place, now under water.

whyWrong.A: Scattered would mean the material had been dispersed, which is close to the washed-out explanation the sentence rules out.
whyWrong.C: Imagined contradicts the physical evidence the trawlers are hauling up.
whyWrong.D: Quarried would mean the landscape had been dug out and removed, and nothing suggests any extraction.

commonMistakes: The blank must contrast with "rubbish washed out from the shore," so any word implying displacement is wrong.

whyCorrect: The text opens with a failure and diagnoses it — the problem was storage at the destination, not the voyage. It then lists what Tudor changed: insulated icehouses, sawdust packing, and free chilled drinks to create demand. It closes with ice among the state's largest exports. That is a failure turned viable by changes in storage and in demand.

whyWrong.A: Timber is mentioned only as the source of the sawdust; no comparison of trades is made.
whyWrong.B: Martinique appears once as the destination of the first shipment, and the passage follows Tudor's business rather than the island's imports.
whyWrong.D: The insulating physics of sawdust is never explained; the sawdust is named as one of the practical fixes.

tips: A purpose question is answered by the arc of the whole passage — problem, response, outcome — not by any single detail in it.

whyCorrect: The sentence before establishes the challenge — flying where the air holds a third of the sea-level oxygen — and the sentence after reports the performance, wingbeats a lowland goose cannot sustain. The underlined sentence sits between them and names the two physiological features, tighter oxygen binding and capillaries closer to the muscle fibres, that make that performance possible.

whyWrong.B: No route is given; the sentence describes the birds' blood and muscle, not their path across the mountains.
whyWrong.C: The sentence supports the account of high flight rather than casting doubt on it.
whyWrong.D: The chamber appears in the following sentence, and the underlined sentence says nothing about how its oxygen level was set.

tips: A sentence sandwiched between a challenge and a result is usually the explanation that links them.

whyCorrect: Everything in the passage turns on the angles. Because the cubes are set at slightly different tilts, different ones catch the window light as a visitor moves, so the gold appears to travel across the vault. The final sentence gives the control case: the same material set flush produces one hard glare and no movement.

whyWrong.A: No comparison with Roman work or with working speed appears anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.B: The apse is simply the setting; the passage never ranks the difficulty of decorating different parts of a church.
whyWrong.C: The purity of the gold is not discussed — what matters is the leaf's orientation, not its quality.

tips: When a passage ends by describing what happens if you do the opposite, that contrast is pointing at the main idea.

whyCorrect: The objection recorded was that the ramps would serve very few people. The counts answer it: most users were pushing prams, wheeling luggage or trolleys, or riding bicycles, and the closing lines note that these people already existed and had been lifting and dragging. The point is that the ramps served far more people than the campaigners themselves.

whyWrong.A: The stated objection was expense against a small number of beneficiaries, not appearance.
whyWrong.B: The counts found the opposite: most users were people with prams, luggage, trolleys or bicycles.
whyWrong.D: The passage places the campaign in Berkeley in the 1970s but never claims it was the first city to install ramps.

commonMistakes: Choice B reverses the passage's finding; read the list of who was actually counted before choosing.

whyCorrect: Wenzel's claim is about where the metal came from, and lead isotope ratios are the standard way of tying finished metal to a particular ore body. A blade whose ratios match southern Alpine ores within a few days' walk and do not match Balkan ores points the source to the place he died, which is exactly what she argues.

whyWrong.B: Axes of similar shape across central Europe show a shared design, and a design can travel without the metal doing so.
whyWrong.C: The yew haft says where the wood came from, not where the copper was smelted.
whyWrong.D: Long-distance trade in Balkan copper supports the rival account Wenzel is arguing against.

tips: A provenance claim needs a provenance measurement — look for the choice matching the object's composition to a source.

whyCorrect: Nakamura's claim is about what the device was for. Evidence of purpose has to come from what Scott did with it, and choice C gives two such things: notebooks pairing tracings with the vowels spoken and comparing their shapes, and a petition to have the device used in teaching shorthand. Both are uses of the traces as visible records of speech, with no playback intended.

whyWrong.A: Access to acoustics literature explains how he knew the field, not what he built the instrument to do.
whyWrong.B: Edison's later machine shows what someone else wanted from sound recording and says nothing about Scott's intention.
whyWrong.D: Modern reconstruction shows the tracings happen to contain enough information for playback, which is about what the traces are, not what Scott designed them for.

commonMistakes: A claim about intent is supported by the inventor's own practice, not by what the device turned out to be capable of later.

whyCorrect: Halvorsen has to show the blooms cause melting rather than merely accompanying it, which means intervening on the algae and seeing the melting change. Choice A does that: plots with the algae suppressed reflected about a seventh more sunlight and lost less depth than untreated plots beside them. Same conditions, only the algae removed, different melting.

whyWrong.B: Earlier blooms in warm springs is exactly the symptom pattern he is arguing against — warmth causing algae rather than algae causing melt.
whyWrong.C: A wide geographic distribution shows the algae are common, not that they drive melting.
whyWrong.D: Overwintering explains how the blooms return each year and says nothing about their effect on melt.

tips: To separate cause from symptom, look for the choice in which the suspected cause is removed and the effect changes.

whyCorrect: The passage names the exact obstacle: a film of water sits between glue and surface, and nothing bonds through it. The larva's first secretion is oily and spreads out ahead of the cement, so it reaches the surface before the cement does. Its most likely job is to push that water film aside and clear the way.

whyWrong.A: Predators are never mentioned, and an oil layer spreading under the cement would not shield anything.
whyWrong.B: The cement is what forms the bond; the oily phase is described as a separate, earlier secretion.
whyWrong.D: No dissolving of rock is described, and etching the surface would not address the water film the passage identifies as the problem.

tips: When a passage states a specific obstacle and then describes a first step, the step is almost always aimed at that obstacle.

whyCorrect: The zeolite works as a fixed sieve: narrower molecules go in, wider ones cannot. To separate two gases you need one to be admitted and the other excluded, so the channel has to be wider than one molecule and narrower than the other — that is, intermediate between them.

whyWrong.B: Channels narrower than both molecules would admit neither, so nothing would be separated.
whyWrong.C: The passage states that the width does not change with temperature or pressure, so this is ruled out.
whyWrong.D: Channels wider than both would admit both, again leaving the mixture unseparated.

commonMistakes: Students pick the option that lets the target gas in without checking that the other gas must be kept out.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is the carver's name, and "a man who worked in ivory and boxwood in nineteenth-century Osaka" is an appositive describing him. It opened with a comma after his name, so it has to close with a comma before the verb "arranged."

whyWrong.A: Without the closing comma the appositive is left open and runs straight into the main verb.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and "arranged his figures so that every limb folds back" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon also requires a complete clause before it, and a subject with an unclosed appositive is not one.

tips: Long appositives are easy to lose track of — find the comma that opened it before deciding what closes it.

whyCorrect: "Blue clay and a cap of turf sealed the mound and kept the air out of it" is a complete sentence, and "the wood, the textiles and a wooden cart came out of it in a condition no ordinary grave would have left them in" is another. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them are joined by a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into one run-on sentence.
whyWrong.B: A colon is never followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause reports a result rather than an explanation.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice; the commas later in the sentence separate list items, not clauses.

commonMistakes: The list "the wood, the textiles and a wooden cart" makes the second clause look like a continuation of the first — check for its own verb, "came out."

whyCorrect: A dash has already been opened after "so far" to introduce the list of proposed explanations. That list interrupts the sentence between its subject, "Every explanation offered so far," and its verb, "predicts," so the interruption must be closed with a matching dash.

whyWrong.B: A comma cannot close a dash, and the marks in a parenthetical pair have to match.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon cannot close a dash either, and it would need a complete clause on each side.
whyWrong.D: A colon cannot close a dash, and the material after it is the sentence's own verb phrase rather than an explanation.

tips: When you see an opening dash before the blank, the answer is almost always the closing dash.

whyCorrect: "Although" makes everything up to "four feet deep" a dependent clause, and the main clause is "freight rates between the Great Lakes and New York fell by something like ninety per cent." A dependent clause that opens a sentence is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and the "Although" clause is dependent.
whyWrong.B: A colon has the same requirement on its left, which the "Although" clause does not meet.
whyWrong.C: "And" pulls the main clause into the "Although" clause, leaving the sentence a fragment.

tips: "Although," "because," "while" and "since" all create dependent clauses — none of them can sit on the left of a semicolon or colon.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists what the grant is for, and the first two items are infinitives: "to strip the lead paint" and "to light the frame from below." The item after "and" is the third in that series, so it must take the same form — "to open the ground inside it to the public."

whyWrong.A: "Having opened" is a perfect participle and places the opening before the other two actions, which breaks both the parallelism and the sense.
whyWrong.B: "Opening" is a gerund or participle rather than an infinitive, so the third item no longer matches the first two.
whyWrong.D: "It opens" is a full clause, which cannot be the third item in a list of infinitive phrases.

tips: Read back to the first item in the list before choosing — parallelism is set by the series, not by the nearest words.

whyCorrect: Two past events are being ordered. The inspectors' arrival in April is the later one, and the thinning of the ice happened before they got there. English marks the earlier of two past events with the past perfect, so "had thinned" is required.

whyWrong.B: "Will thin" is future and cannot describe something already true at a past moment.
whyWrong.C: "Is thinning" places the process in the present, contradicting "By the time the inspectors reached."
whyWrong.D: "Thins" is a simple present describing a general habit, not a specific completed change before a past arrival.

tips: "By the time" plus a simple past clause is a reliable cue for the past perfect in the other clause.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The museum's collection," which is singular. "Together with several hundred trade catalogues" is a parenthetical phrase and does not make the subject plural. The move happened last winter, so the verb is the singular past passive "was moved."

whyWrong.A: "Are" is plural and also present, wrong on both counts for a completed move last winter.
whyWrong.B: "Have been" is plural and shifts to the present perfect, which sits awkwardly with the specific past time "last winter."
whyWrong.C: "Were" is plural and agrees with "catalogues," a noun inside the parenthetical phrase rather than the subject.

commonMistakes: "Together with," "as well as" and "along with" never turn a singular subject plural — only "and" does that.

whyCorrect: The first sentence lists the technology's advantage: it keeps an image with no power, so a page costs nothing to display for a week. The second introduces the drawback — redrawing is slow — and draws the limit that follows from it. Advantage then drawback is a contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make the slow refresh a consequence of holding an image without power, but the second sentence sets a limitation against the first rather than deriving from it.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" says the two sentences agree, and they point in opposite directions.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would make slowness an example of the power-free advantage, which it is not.

tips: When one sentence praises and the next restricts, you need a contrast word even if a causal one sounds plausible.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the physical fact: the train is held clear of the guideway and nothing touches anything. The second states what follows — the wear that dominates a conventional railway's maintenance bill never arises. No contact is the cause and no wear is the effect.

whyWrong.B: "By contrast" would set the second sentence against the first, but it follows from it.
whyWrong.C: "In other words" signals a restatement, and the absence of wear is a consequence rather than a rephrasing of magnetic levitation.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" would mean the wear is absent despite the lack of contact, which reverses the logic.

tips: If the second sentence would not be true without the first, the transition marks a result.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the old stocks, printed to a pale reference, and their failure on darker skin. The second describes the reformulated stocks, which held detail across a far wider range of tones. Two stocks, opposite results — the transition marks the comparison.

whyWrong.A: "For example" would make the reformulated stocks an instance of the earlier problem, but they are the case where the problem is fixed.
whyWrong.C: "Consequently" would say the improvement followed from the bias itself; the passage credits pressure from furniture and chocolate advertisers.
whyWrong.D: "In addition" adds a further point in the same direction, and the second sentence points the other way.

commonMistakes: The reason given inside the second sentence is advertiser pressure, not the earlier failure — so the link between the sentences is not causal.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why place-names are useful evidence, which needs the weakness of the alternative source and the property that makes names reliable. Choice A supplies both: the written records are thin and hostile, and names stay attached to the land through changes of ownership, so they map where Norse speakers settled.

whyWrong.B: The unreliability of the chronicles explains why another source is needed but never says what makes names good evidence.
whyWrong.C: The endings and their language of origin are the raw data, not an account of their evidential value.
whyWrong.D: The distribution across counties is a result obtained from the names rather than a reason for trusting them.

tips: A "why is X useful evidence" goal usually needs two notes: the gap in other sources and the property that fills it.

whyCorrect: The goal is about how the outcome was kept unfixed, so the sentence needs the features that defeat manipulation. Choice D names both: each ball took or rejected a whole row of tokens at once, and the order of the balls could not be known beforehand, so no official could arrange who was chosen.

whyWrong.A: Slotting tokens into the columns describes the setup and shows nothing about unpredictability.
whyWrong.B: A physical description of the slab and tube says what the device was, not how it resisted fixing.
whyWrong.C: That offices were filled by lot is the context; it does not explain how this particular device made the lot secure.

commonMistakes: Descriptive notes about the apparatus feel relevant, but only the two notes about randomness answer a goal about preventing a fixed outcome.

whyCorrect: To emphasise how fast the service was made obsolete you need the two dates side by side. Choice A puts the April 1860 opening against the closure announced two days after the telegraph was completed in October 1861, which shows the whole life of the service and how abruptly it ended.

whyWrong.B: The telegraph's completion date alone gives no sense of what it displaced or how quickly.
whyWrong.C: The postage rate says what the service cost, not how long it lasted.
whyWrong.D: The stations and horses describe the scale of the operation without any reference to its end.

tips: When a goal is about speed or timing, the right choice will contain the dates that bracket the change.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up a contradiction — the animal matches colours yet tests show it has one visual pigment and is colour blind — and the clause after the blank says no explanation offered has won general agreement. The blank therefore names a question still open.

whyWrong.B: Exaggerated would mean the colour-matching has been overstated, but the passage reports it as established fact.
whyWrong.C: Undisputed is the opposite of what the sentence's second half says, since no explanation has been agreed on.
whyWrong.D: Trivial conflicts with a puzzle presented as important enough to have drawn competing explanations.

tips: The clause after the blank usually fixes the answer — here "no explanation yet offered has won general agreement" defines the word you need.

whyCorrect: The passage insists that nothing is manufactured at the moment of need: the threads already exist, packed in glands along the flank. What seawater does is turn a thimbleful into litres of gel in a fraction of a second, which means the stored threads are unpacking rather than being made. "Unfurled" names that expansion of something already formed.

whyWrong.A: Concealed reverses the action — the threads are being released into the water, not hidden.
whyWrong.B: Hardened describes a change of consistency, but what the passage measures is a change of volume into a clogging gel.
whyWrong.D: Consumed would mean the threads are used up as fuel, and they are the material of the defence itself.

commonMistakes: The sentence's job is to say what seawater does to ready-made threads, so any word implying creation or destruction misses the point.

whyCorrect: The passage explains that peat is cold, acid and almost oxygen-free, which halts the bacteria that spoil food, and notes that some of the buried fat is still edible after three thousand years. Burial that keeps food fit to eat is putting it away for later, which the sentence contrasts with disposal.

whyWrong.A: Ceremony would make the burial symbolic, and the passage gives a purely practical account of why the contents survive.
whyWrong.B: Waste is a synonym for the disposal the sentence explicitly rules out.
whyWrong.D: Concealment would explain hiding the vessels but not why the text dwells on the chemistry that keeps the fat edible.

tips: In "not X but _____," test each option by asking whether the passage's evidence supports it over X.

whyCorrect: The described feathers do one job: they take up water at the waterhole and grip it against the pull of the air for fifty kilometres. The barbs coiling when dry and uncoiling in water is a water-holding mechanism, so the plumage is functioning as something that carries a liquid rather than as body covering.

whyWrong.A: Ballast is weight carried for stability, and the water is being transported for use rather than to trim the bird.
whyWrong.B: Insulation is the ordinary function of plumage, which is what the sentence is setting the described role against.
whyWrong.C: Camouflage concerns appearance, and nothing about colour or concealment appears in the passage.

tips: "Less as X than as _____" requires the blank to name the special function just demonstrated, not the default one.

whyCorrect: One process produces both properties: the skin sets first and the interior contracts afterwards, leaving the surface in compression and the core in tension. That squeezed surface is what survives a hammer blow, and that stored strain is what shatters the drop when the tail is snipped. Strength and fragility are two results of the same arrangement.

whyWrong.A: Substitutes would mean one stands in for the other, but the drop is both strong and fragile at once.
whyWrong.C: Measurements would make them quantities of the arrangement rather than effects produced by it.
whyWrong.D: Exceptions implies they depart from the arrangement, whereas they follow directly from it.

commonMistakes: The sentence denies that the two are opposites, so the answer must be a word that lets both come from one cause.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets the problem — a micron-wide bead cannot be picked up with anything solid. The last describes what biologists do with the technique. The underlined sentence in between supplies the physics that bridges them: light carries momentum, and a bead near the beam waist is pushed back towards the brightest point whenever it drifts. Without that principle the applications would not follow.

whyWrong.A: The choice of glass is never justified; the sentence explains the trapping force, not the material.
whyWrong.C: The organisms — a bacterium, a strand of DNA — are named in the final sentence, not the underlined one.
whyWrong.D: No limitation is conceded; the sentence describes the mechanism that makes the trap work.

tips: A sentence standing between a problem and its uses is nearly always the principle that connects them.

whyCorrect: The passage opens with a requirement — small enough to fly and powerful enough to return an echo — and states that existing valves could deliver only one of the two. It then describes the cavity magnetron, fist-sized and more powerful at short wavelengths than anything in service, and notes that airborne sets followed within two years. Requirement unmet, then device that meets it.

whyWrong.B: No other country's radar is mentioned, so no comparison of national systems is made.
whyWrong.C: Valves appear only as the inadequate existing option; their history is not traced.
whyWrong.D: How range is derived from echo timing is never explained; the passage is about generating the signal, not interpreting it.

tips: When a text opens by naming two requirements that conflict, its purpose is usually to present whatever resolved the conflict.

whyCorrect: The aviary result is the key: birds dig in the right places when the landmarks are undisturbed and in predictably shifted places when the landmarks are moved. Errors that follow the displacement show the birds are working from positions relative to those landmarks, which is how they find tens of thousands of caches months later.

whyWrong.A: Smell is never mentioned, and it could not explain digging that shifts when landmarks are moved — nor would it work through fresh snow.
whyWrong.C: The text says the birds recover most of their caches, not that many are lost.
whyWrong.D: The pines' side of the relationship is not discussed at all; the passage is about how the bird remembers.

tips: When an experiment reports errors that track a manipulation, those errors identify the cue the animal was using.

whyCorrect: Two claims run through the passage. The design is subtractive — nothing is applied, and the pattern exists only where cloth has been cut away. And the standard of quality is the hemming on the reverse, which is why a Guna woman turns the panel over to judge it. Choice B is the only option that holds both.

whyWrong.A: The passage gives a number of layers, three or four, but says nothing about change over time.
whyWrong.C: Colours are mentioned only as the differing layers that the cutting reveals, with no preference stated.
whyWrong.D: No comparison with embroidery or with the time either method takes appears in the text.

commonMistakes: A main-idea answer has to cover the whole passage; a choice that captures only the cutting or only the judging is too narrow.

whyCorrect: Raghavan claims the height is a requirement of the fungus, not an accident. That means the fungus must do worse when the height changes. Choice D provides it: fungi fruiting at other heights infected far fewer ants than those at about twenty-five centimetres, where humidity and temperature suit the fungus best. The variable is moved and the fungus pays for it.

whyWrong.A: A range of sapling species shows the behaviour is not tied to one plant, which says nothing about the height mattering.
whyWrong.B: Growing the fungus on laboratory medium shows it does not strictly need an ant, which if anything works against the idea that the ant's position is critical.
whyWrong.C: Uninfected ants climbing saplings makes the behaviour look less unusual rather than showing that the height serves the fungus.

tips: To show a detail is required rather than incidental, look for evidence that changing it makes the outcome worse.

whyCorrect: Ibarra's claim sets the rules against the character of the candidates, so the useful finding holds the candidates constant and changes the rules. Choice B does exactly that: the same people who ran negative advertisements under plurality rules ran far fewer after the switch. If the candidates did not change and the behaviour did, the rules are doing the work.

whyWrong.A: Counting time is an administrative fact with no bearing on why campaigns are less hostile.
whyWrong.C: Greater satisfaction with outcomes is a result of the system but does not separate the rules from the candidates.
whyWrong.D: Higher turnout again shows an effect of the system without addressing which of the two proposed causes produces the civility.

commonMistakes: Several choices are true consequences of ranked ballots; only one controls for the rival explanation the argument names.

whyCorrect: Lu's claim is about the writers' business organisation: standing establishments rather than travelling peddling. Instructions to collect debts owed at named addresses and to hold goods in a warehouse until prices rise imply fixed premises, credit extended over time and someone on the spot to act — all things an itinerant peddler does not have.

whyWrong.A: The writing surface tells you about materials available, not about how the businesses were organised.
whyWrong.B: The wide use of Sogdian in trade explains the language of the letters and nothing about permanent establishments.
whyWrong.C: The watchtower's position on the main route explains where the letters were intercepted, not how the merchants operated.

tips: For a claim about how people were organised, look for evidence of their standing arrangements — premises, credit, staff — rather than their setting.

whyCorrect: The trap works because dry sand is already at the steepest angle it can hold, so an ant's step removes the grains beneath it and starts a slide. The passage says damp sand holds a much steeper face without slipping — so a wall of damp sand would be well short of its limit and would simply bear the ant's weight instead of collapsing.

whyWrong.A: Damp sand is more stable than dry, so if anything the walls would stand better during digging, not collapse.
whyWrong.C: Excavation time is not what the passage is about, and a slower dig would not change whether the trap works.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the mechanism: it is the instability of dry sand at its maximum angle that catches the ant.

commonMistakes: Damp sand sounds like the better building material, and it is — which is exactly why it makes a worse trap.

whyCorrect: The passage gives the reasoning rule directly: a signal from a particular source would vary as the antenna turned. The hiss did not vary with direction, with the pigeons removed, or through the seasons. A signal that is the same whichever way you point must be arriving equally from every direction.

whyWrong.A: A source directly overhead is still a particular direction, so the hiss would change as the horn turned away from it.
whyWrong.C: An intermittent fault would come and go, whereas the hiss was constant over seasons.
whyWrong.D: A source inside the antenna is what clearing out the pigeons and checking the equipment was meant to rule out, and it would not be described as a source in the sky.

tips: When a passage states what a rival hypothesis would predict, check each choice against that prediction.

whyCorrect: "Bessemer's converter blew cold air up through tonnes of molten pig iron and delivered three things at once" is a complete clause that announces a list, and what follows is that list — a metal with the carbon burned out, a charge that stayed hot, and a batch finished in twenty minutes. A colon introduces a list after a complete clause.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and "a metal with the carbon burned out of it" is a noun phrase.
whyWrong.C: "And" makes the metal a coordinate element of the preceding clause, leaving the other two items with nothing to attach to.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the list runs straight into the clause and "three things at once a metal" is unreadable.

tips: "Three things," "the following," "two reasons" — a counted announcement takes a colon.

whyCorrect: "Riders take the bikes downhill and towards work in the morning" is a complete sentence, and "vans carry them back up the hill and out to the residential streets overnight" is another. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them are joined with a semicolon.

whyWrong.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation "morning vans" reads as a compound noun and the second clause loses its subject.
whyWrong.D: A colon cannot be followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause is a parallel action rather than an explanation of the first.

commonMistakes: Because the two clauses describe halves of one daily cycle, a comma feels natural — it still splices two sentences.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is already a complete sentence, and what follows explains the phrase "the one thing a fight would make obvious" — namely that the blows are thrown to be seen and pulled before they land. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces such an explanation.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the explanation runs into the clause and "obvious the blows" reads as nonsense.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon followed by "and" doubles the join, and the second clause explains the first rather than merely standing beside it.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

tips: When the second half tells you what a vague phrase in the first half means, the mark between them is a colon.

whyCorrect: The subject is "Anna Atkins," and "a botanist who had been trained to draw specimens by hand" is an appositive describing her. It opened with a comma after her name, so it must close with a comma before the main verb "laid."

whyWrong.A: Without the closing comma the appositive never ends and "hand laid seaweed" reads as a single phrase.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and "laid seaweed directly onto the paper and issued the results in 1843" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon also requires a complete clause before it, which a subject plus an unclosed appositive is not.

tips: Find the comma that opened the appositive; the blank almost always supplies its partner.
